text: PII means personally identifiable information, but not every identifying field works the same way. This lesson splits PII into two very different categories, and introduces a research finding that makes the dangerous one concrete.

Direct identifiers point at exactly one person on their own: a full name, a Social Security number, a passport number, an email address, a phone number. These get flagged immediately in almost any security or privacy review. Quasi-identifiers are the dangerous ones, because they don't look dangerous individually. A ZIP code alone doesn't identify you; a birth date alone doesn't either. But combine a small number of them, and they can narrow a dataset down to one specific person, even after every direct identifier has been stripped out.

Computer scientist Latanya Sweeney made this concrete in 2000. Her research showed that just three widely available fields, a five-digit ZIP code, full date of birth, and gender, uniquely identify a large majority of the U.S. population. Strip the name and Social Security number from a dataset, and it can still re-identify most of the people in it as long as those three quasi-identifiers survive. That's why an 'anonymized' dataset that still carries ZIP, birth date, and gender often isn't anonymous at all.

PII is a U.S.-centric term, and it's narrower than it sounds. GDPR uses a broader concept: personal data, any information relating to an identified or identifiable person. That catches things many PII definitions miss entirely: an IP address, a device ID, a cookie identifier, location history. And a subset of personal data, health information, biometric data, detailed financial accounts, gets treated as special category data under GDPR, with stricter rules than ordinary personal data. That subset is next lesson's full topic.
Direct identifiers are the obvious ones; quasi-identifiers are the ones that bite you later. Next up: sensitive and confidential data, where special category data gets its full treatment.
